title: Why weren't you Zusya?
hookLine: Rabbi Zusya fears heaven won't ask why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya (Hasidic tale)

cards: Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better than you. A better cook. A better parent.
Someone your age who's already written the book, run the marathon, started the company. It's easy to feel like you're failing at being them.
The Hasidic tales of Eastern Europe tell of a rabbi named Zusya, known for being poor, humble and full of joy. Near the end of his life, his students find him weeping, afraid. They're amazed.
What could a man like Zusya possibly fear?

teach.b: Rabbi, the students say, why are you afraid? You've been as faithful as Moses. As kind as Abraham.

And Zusya answers: when I come before the heavenly court, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? I'd have an answer for that: I wasn't given what Moses was given. They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham?
I wasn't Abraham. They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say then?
The story comes from the Hasidim, a movement of joyful, mystical renewal among the Jews of Eastern Europe.
Their stories were told aloud before anyone wrote them down, and later collectors, Martin Buber among them, carried this one into print. Notice what Zusya refuses to do.
Measure yourself against the greatest person you can imagine, and anyone comes up short. Zusya says that isn't the test. Nobody will ask you to be Moses.
The question is harder and kinder at once: did you become the person only you could be? Did you use what you were actually given, your hands, your voice, your odd mix of gifts and wounds?
Harder, because you can't hide behind I'm not Moses. Kinder, because nobody is asking you to be anyone else.
Zusya couldn't answer for Moses. He could only answer for Zusya.

how: Zusya's question is retold in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Hasidic tales like it are still passed on aloud in Hasidic communities.

o: a prophet who stood before the heavenly court
the founder of the Hasidic movement
a humble Hasidic rabbi known for his joy

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: you've been as faithful as Moses

s: Zusya feared being asked why he wasn't Moses
he had an answer for that. he feared being asked why he wasn't Zusya.
Hasidic tales were told aloud before being written down
they were collected later, in books like Martin Buber's.
the story tells you to become someone greater
it asks whether you became the one person only you could be.

games.q: you're Zusya's student. your beloved teacher is weeping, afraid of the heavenly court. what do you say?
o: you've been as faithful as Moses; why fear?
games.why: they praise him as Moses, and he answers: they won't ask me why I wasn't Moses. they'll ask me why I wasn't Zusya.

practice: Let go of the person you've been comparing yourself to; let them walk off. Then ask quietly: what do I have that's mine?
A way of making people laugh, a particular kindness, something you notice that others don't: hold one, and picture one small way to use it, the way only you would.

wordCard.voice: Zusya. A Hasidic rabbi who feared one question: not why weren't you someone greater, but why weren't you yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: be zusya. The only question is the one with your own name in it. That's day fifty-nine.

sources.work: Hasidic tales (oral tradition; collected later, e.g. Martin Buber, Tales of the Hasidim)
